Light Alignment Improves LLM Safety via Model
Self-Reflection with a Single Neuron

Abstract

The safety of large language models (LLMs) has increasingly emerged as a fundamental aspect of their development. Existing safety alignment for LLMs is predominantly achieved through post-training methods, which are computationally expensive and often fail to generalize well across different models. A small number of lightweight alignment approaches either rely heavily on prior-computed safety injections or depend excessively on the model’s own capabilities, resulting in limited generalization and degraded efficiency and usability during generation.

In this work, we propose a safety-aware decoding method that requires only low-cost training of an expert model and employs a single neuron as a gating mechanism. By effectively balancing the model’s intrinsic capabilities with external guidance, our approach simultaneously preserves utility and enhances output safety. It demonstrates clear advantages in training overhead and generalization across model scales, offering a new perspective on lightweight alignment for the safe and practical deployment of large language models. Code: https://github.com/Beijing-AISI/NGSD.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, the safety of their generated outputs has become a central dimension for evaluating overall model capability. The continued scaling of model size and expressive power enables flexible generation under complex instructions, but simultaneously amplifies the risk of producing unsafe, harmful, or value-misaligned content (Ouyang et al., 2022). Ensuring that LLMs reliably adhere to safety constraints during generation without substantially compromising utility—has therefore emerged as a key challenge in contemporary language model research (Perez et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024b). Importantly, this challenge is no longer confined to adversarial or edge-case inputs; safety violations increasingly arise in open-ended and seemingly benign usage scenarios, where risks are harder to anticipate and control.

Most existing work formulates this challenge as an alignment problem, aiming to align model behavior with human values, usage norms, and safety boundaries. The dominant solutions rely on post-training paradigms, such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning-based methods, which explicitly encode safety into model parameters (Wang et al., 2024c). These approaches have proven effective in practice, particularly in reducing overtly harmful behaviors (e.g., RLHF and DPO) (Sharma et al., 2025b; Rafailov et al., 2023). However, post-training alignment is computationally expensive, heavily dependent on large-scale, carefully curated human preference data, and typically requires full or partial fine-tuning for each target model or checkpoint (Wang et al., 2024a; Lin et al., 2024). As a result, alignment becomes tightly coupled with costly retraining pipelines, limiting scalability and hindering efficient reuse across model families (Ding and Wang, 2025; Li et al., 2024a).

To mitigate these limitations, a growing line of research has shifted attention to inference-time safety mechanisms, which intervene directly during decoding without modifying model parameters. From a design perspective, existing approaches can be broadly categorized into three groups. The first group relies on external intervention, injecting safety constraints by steering hidden representations along predefined safety-related directions or by modifying output probabilities using expert models or safety vectors (Shen et al., 2024; Banerjee et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024b). The second group formulates safe generation as a constrained search problem, employing handcrafted rules, rollback strategies, or tree-based exploration to identify token sequences that satisfy safety constraints (Li et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025a). In parallel, a third line of work relies almost entirely on the model’s intrinsic capabilities, prompting the model to reflect, self-examine, or proactively refuse unsafe requests during generation (Zhang et al., 2025b; Phute et al., 2023). Existing inference-time safety methods face fundamental limitations. Approaches based on external intervention or search often avoid model post-training and incur minimal inference-time overhead; however, they typically require substantial model-specific pre-computation, such as constructing auxiliary datasets or deriving safety vectors for each target model, which introduces non-trivial deployment overhead and poor cross-model generalization. In contrast, methods relying solely on model self-reflection are lightweight at both training and inference time, but depend on unreliable and highly model-specific safety awareness. More fundamentally, current external intervention methods fail to utilize the target model’s intrinsic safety capabilities learned during training, resulting in redundant and inefficient interventions even when inputs are already recognized as safe (Huang et al., 2025; Han et al., 2025).

Building on this insight, we propose a lightweight Neuron Guided Safe Decoding (termed NGSD) that explicitly couples intrinsic model awareness with minimal external control. Our approach requires training only the smallest model in a model family as a safety expert, substantially reducing alignment cost while enabling efficient transfer to larger, related models. At the core of our method, we introduce a single-neuron-based gating mechanism that exposes the model’s internal risk signals and adaptively regulates safety intervention during decoding. As a result, safety control is selectively activated only when elevated risk is detected, rather than being uniformly imposed. This design preserves model utility on benign inputs while maintaining robust safety behavior, achieving an effective balance between intrinsic model capability and external guidance. The main contributions of this work are threefold:

  • •

    NGSD introduces a lightweight decoding-time safety alignment algorithm that requires training only a single expert model at the smallest scale, enabling efficient and low-cost transfer across model families.

  • •

    NGSD proposes a single-neuron-based gating mechanism that explicitly couples the model’s intrinsic risk awareness with external safety control, allowing safety constraints to be applied adaptively and only when necessary, rather than through uniform or heuristic intervention.

  • •

    Through extensive experiments across multiple safety and utility benchmarks, we demonstrate that our method exhibits strong generalization and transferability, while consistently achieving a favorable safety–utility trade-off compared to strong inference-time baselines.

2 Related Work

2.1 Jailbreak Attack

Jailbreak attacks aim to bypass the safety alignment mechanisms of large language models to elicit unsafe or harmful outputs. Early studies mainly rely on manually crafted adversarial prompts that exploit conflicts between safety and helpfulness objectives or reveal generalization failures under adversarial input distributions (Mowshowitz, 2022; Zeng et al., 2024). While effective, such approaches are limited in scalability. More recent work shifts toward automated, optimization-based jailbreak generation. Gradient-based methods, such as GCG (Zou et al., 2023), optimize adversarial prefixes to identify trigger tokens that induce unsafe responses, whereas search- or evolution-based approaches like AutoDAN (Liu et al., 2023) explore the discrete prompt space without gradient access. In parallel, red-teaming frameworks introduce auxiliary language models to iteratively generate and refine jailbreak prompts through multi-round interactions, as exemplified by PAIR (Chao et al., 2025) and GPTFuzzer (Yu et al., 2023). These advances motivate the need for alignment methods specifically designed to defend against increasingly automated jailbreak attacks.

2.2 Decoding-time Safety Methods

Early alignment methods predominantly operate at the post-training stage, where model weights are fine-tuned on safety datasets aligned with human preferences. InstructGPT (Ouyang et al., 2022) combines supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning from human feedback, while later approaches such as DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023), PITA (Bobbili et al., 2025), and DRPO (Singla et al., 2024) reduce annotation dependence or introduce preference-based and prompt-aware optimization. Despite their effectiveness, these methods incur high training costs that scale with model size and require model-specific alignment, limiting generalization.

In contrast, decoding-time alignment methods enforce safety during generation. Approaches such as Jailbreak Antidote (Shen et al., 2024), SafeInfer (Banerjee et al., 2025), and InferAligner (Wang et al., 2024b) inject safety-related guidance into model representations, whereas RAIN (Li et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025a) frames safe generation as a constrained token-level search problem. Although these methods reduce training overhead, they often introduce additional computation at inference time, degrade utility, and still exhibit limited cross-model generalization.

2.3 Leveraging Intrinsic Model Capabilities for Safety

In safety-aware generation, the model’s internal risk-awareness capability is relatively underexplored. CARE (Hu et al., 2025) and Bidirectional Intention (Tong et al., 2025) enable periodic self-checks during decoding to detect and roll back unsafe tokens. ICD (Wei et al., 2023), Self-Reminder (Wu et al., 2023), and Self-Exam (Phute et al., 2023) further prompt the model to explicitly recognize harmful intent or re-evaluate its own outputs during generation. In a related vein, Persona-Judge (Zhang et al., 2025a) and PAD (Chen et al., 2024) assign the model dual roles as generator and judge to suppress unsafe tokens via prompt-based or learning-based mechanisms.

3 Preliminary

3.1 Safety-Aware Decoding

As formulated in Eq. 1, SafeDecoding (Xu et al., 2024) ensures output safety by jointly decoding a base model and a safety expert at inference time. The safety expert is obtained via LoRA-based fine-tuning of the base model and therefore shares the same architecture and model scale. At each decoding step tt, the conditional distribution over the next token yty_{t} is adjusted by linearly interpolating the predictions of the base model pbp_{b} and the expert model pep_{e}. The interpolation coefficient α\alpha controls the strength of the safety guidance.

P⁡(ytCLOSE\displaystyle P(y_{t} ∣y<t,x)=pb(yt∣y<t,x)\displaystyle\mid y_{<t},x)=p_{b}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t},x) (1)
+α⁡(pe​(yt∣y<t,x)−pb​(yt∣y<t,x))\displaystyle+\alpha\Big(p_{e}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t},x)-p_{b}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t},x)\Big)

Building upon this framework, Speculative Safety-Aware Decoding (SSD) (Wang et al., 2025b) introduces a lightweight safety expert and constructs either intersection-based or union-based candidate token sets between the base and expert models at each decoding step. Instead of operating on probabilities, SSD directly performs safety-aware adjustments on token log-probabilities within the selected token set. Furthermore, SSD leverages historical decoding signals to periodically adapt the coefficient α\alpha and dynamically switch between different decoding modes, achieving a better balance among safety, efficiency, and utility.

3.2 Nonlinear Neuron as Temporal Gating Mechanism

We propose a neuron-inspired unit (Eq. 2) designed to act as a gating mechanism in the temporal domain.

τm​d​V​(t)d​t=−(V⁡(t)−Vrest)+R​I​(t),\tau_{m}\frac{dV(t)}{dt}=-\big(V(t)-V_{\text{rest}}\big)+RI(t), (2)

where V⁡(t)V(t) denotes the membrane potential, I⁡(t)I(t) is the input signal, and τm\tau_{m} controls the temporal integration scale. This dynamics allows the neuron to retain historical information by accumulating both past and current inputs. A spike is generated when the membrane potential exceeds a predefined threshold,

S⁡(t)=Θ⁡(V⁡(t)−Vth),S(t)=\Theta\big(V(t)-V_{\text{th}}\big), (3)

where Θ⁡(⋅)\Theta(\cdot) denotes the Heaviside step function, which outputs 11 for positive inputs and 00 otherwise. The resulting binary output S⁡(t)∈{0,1}S(t)\in\{0,1\} can be naturally interpreted as a gating signal.

In NGSD, the distributional discrepancy between the target model and the expert model is injected into the neuron as the input signal I⁡(t)I(t). Owing to its nonlinearity, the neuron simultaneously supports the accumulation of historical signals and rapid responses to strong immediate signals. The experimental results prove neurons effective for gating.

4 Methodology

4.1 Overview

We propose Neuron-Guided Safe Decoding (NGSD), a lightweight inference-time alignment framework (Fig. 1). NGSD aims to provide robust safety guarantees under unsafe inputs while preserving the base model’s utility capability on the benign inputs, without modifying model parameters or introducing significant inference-time overhead.

Before decoding, NGSD performs a one-time prompt-level self-reflection, in which the base model evaluates the input prompt along multiple risk dimensions and the algorithm selects a fixed safety guidance strength for the generation process. This design allows the method to adapt safety intensity to the input risk level. During decoding, NGSD employs a neuron-guided gating mechanism to monitor the distributional discrepancy between the base model and a lightweight safety expert, accumulating this signal over time and triggering external safety intervention only when sustained risk is detected. When the gate is activated, NGSD applies SafeDecoding-style logit correction at the current decoding step to combine predictions from the base and expert models; otherwise, decoding proceeds using the base model alone. Through this selective intervention strategy, NGSD enforces safety constraints at high-risk positions while minimizing interference with normal generation.

4.2 Neuron-Guided Decoding

NGSD introduces a lightweight safety expert model MeM_{e} at decoding time to provide external safety guidance for a base model MbM_{b} when necessary. We select the smallest model from the same model family as the base model as the expert, ensuring a shared tokenizer and a compatible output space. The expert model is trained with lightweight safety augmentation and can be directly transferred to larger models within the same family.

Distributional Discrepancy as Risk Signal.

At decoding step tt, given the input prompt xx and the previously generated tokens y<ty_{<t}, we compute the next-token probability distributions of the base and expert models:

pb=softmax⁡(Mb​(x,y<t)),pe=softmax⁡(Me​(x,y<t)).p_{b}=\mathrm{softmax}(M_{b}(x,y_{<t})),\quad p_{e}=\mathrm{softmax}(M_{e}(x,y_{<t})).

We measure the discrepancy between the two distributions using the ℓ1\ell_{1} norm,

I⁡(t)=12​∥pb−pe∥1,I(t)=\frac{1}{2}\lVert p_{b}-p_{e}\rVert_{1},

and treat I⁡(t)I(t) as a scalar risk signal at the current decoding step. Intuitively, a large discrepancy indicates strong disagreement between the base model and the safety expert, suggesting an increased likelihood of unsafe generation.

Neuron-Inspired Gating.

Rather than triggering intervention based on instantaneous discrepancies, NGSD employs a neuron-inspired gating mechanism that takes the distributional discrepancy ItI_{t} as its input and integrates this signal over time. The gate is activated only when sustained risk is detected, enabling NGSD to distinguish persistent tendencies from fluctuations. This design allows safety intervention to be applied selectively, avoiding unnecessary interference at low-risk decoding steps.

Selective SafeDecoding Intervention.

When the neuron gate is activated, NGSD applies SafeDecoding-style logit correction at the current decoding step. Specifically, we construct a candidate token set

C=TopK⁡(pb)∪TopK⁡(pe)C=\mathrm{TopK}(p_{b})\cup\mathrm{TopK}(p_{e}) (4)

and compute the corrected distribution

p~​(y)=pb​(y)+α⁡(pe​(y)−pb​(y)),x∈C\tilde{p}(y)=p_{b}(y)+\alpha\bigl(p_{e}(y)-p_{b}(y)\bigr),\quad x\in C (5)

where α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] denotes the safety guidance strength determined by prompt-level self-reflection (Sec. 4.3). The next token is selected from p~\tilde{p}. If the gate is not activated, decoding proceeds using the base model without modification.

By activating external guidance only at decoding steps associated with sustained risk, NGSD enforces safety constraints at critical positions while preserving the base model’s original generation behavior in the majority of cases.

4.3 Prompt-Level Self-Reflection

As described in Sec. 4.1, NGSD jointly balances and leverages internal and external signals to assess risk and orchestrate effective defense actions. In this subsection, we focus on how the strength of the safety guidance α\alpha–which determines the influence of the safety expert when intervention is triggered–is selected prior to decoding. Larger values of α\alpha enforce stronger safety constraints but may degrade generation quality, while smaller values better preserve the base model’s utility at the cost of weaker safety guarantees. Selecting an appropriate value of α\alpha is therefore critical to balancing safety and utility in decoding-time alignment.

To avoid unstable and computationally expensive token-level parameter adjustments, NGSD adopts a prompt-level self-reflection strategy that determines the safety guidance strength once before decoding begins. Specifically, prior to generation, the base model evaluates the input prompt along multiple predefined risk dimensions that capture objective aspects of risk, rather than being designed for any particular attack method or attack class.

Let S,A,E,T∈[0,10]S,A,E,T\in[0,10] denote the scores for severity, actionability, evasion, and targeting, respectively. To obtain an overall risk estimate, we first sort the set P={A,E,T}P=\{A,E,T\} in descending order and denote the two largest values as P1P_{1} and P2P_{2}. The aggregated risk score rr is then computed as

r=max⁡(S,12​S+12⋅P1+P22)r=\max\!\left(S,\;\frac{1}{2}S+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{P_{1}+P_{2}}{2}\right) (6)

which is then clipped to range [0,10][0,10].

Based on the resulting risk score, NGSD selects a fixed safety guidance strength for the entire decoding procss: α\alpha in Eq. 5 is set to 0.90.9 for high-risk prompts (r>5r>5) and to 0.10.1 for low-risk prompts (r≤5r\leq 5). Once decoding starts, α\alpha remains constant throughout generation. Self-reflection avoids periodic parameter updates and additional inference overhead required by prior methods such as SSD, while still allowing the strength of safety intervention to adapt to the input prompt. Combined with neuron-gated decoding, this design provides an efficient mechanism for enhancing safety during generation. The complete decoding procedure is summarized in Algorithm 1. The rationale behind the choice of dimensions and the score aggregation is provided in the Appendix. B.2.

5 Experiment

5.1 Experiment Setup

Target & Expert Models.

We consider two representative model families, Llama and Qwen3. For Llama, we evaluate Llama-2–based targets (Llama-2-7B/13B-chat-hf and Vicuna-7B-v1.5)(Touvron et al., 2023; Chiang et al., 2023) and a Llama-3–based target (Llama3.1-8B-Instruct) (Dubey et al., 2024), and further include Qwen3-8B to test robustness beyond the Llama backbone (Yang et al., 2025). Following a lightweight, family-consistent protocol, Llama-2 targets share TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0 as the expert (Zhang et al., 2024), while Llama-3 and Qwen3 targets use the smallest available models in-family (Llama3.2-1B-Instruct and Qwen3-1B). Crucially, our expert setup is identical to SSD, isolating gains to the decoding algorithm rather than expert design, training, or data. All experts are trained with DeepAlign (Qi et al., 2024) on the corresponding Safety Augmentation datasets.

Datasets & Metrics

We evaluate our method along three dimensions—safety, utility, and over-refusal—to demonstrate the effectiveness of NGSD, as well as its strong transferability and robustness across different target models and attack methods. See more details in Appendix. 7- B.6

Safety is evaluated using the automated framework of (Qi et al., 2023), with Qwen-max (Bai et al., 2023) as the judge model. Given a prompt–response pair, the judge assigns a harmfulness score from 1 (harmless) to 5 (highly harmful). We report the average harmfulness score and the Attack Success Rate (ASR), defined as the fraction of prompts that elicit harmful responses.

Utility is assessed on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), Just-Eval (Lin et al., 2023), and Alpaca-Eval (Dubois et al., 2025). GSM8K evaluates mathematical reasoning and is challenging for composite decoding due to limited baseline performance; we report ROUGE scores and correctness judged by GPT-3.5-turbo. Just-Eval and Alpaca-Eval measure instruction-following quality across multiple dimensions (e.g., helpfulness, clarity, and factuality) following standard protocols.

Over-refusal quantifies incorrect rejections of benign but sensitive requests. We evaluate on XSTest (Röttger et al., 2024) and FalseReject (Zhang et al., 2025b), reporting the False Refusal Rate (FRR) under both LLM-based and string-matching judgments, where lower FRR indicates better discrimination between harmful and legitimate inputs.

5.2 Experiment Result

5.2.1 Safety Robustness and Generalization

As shown in Tab. 1, our method demonstrates stable and consistent safety performance across a wide range of model–attack combinations, outperforming existing baselines in most settings. Even when it does not exceed the strongest baseline under certain configurations, it remains competitive and consistently outperforms SafeDecoding-based defenses on average.

On weakly or moderately aligned models such as Vicuna and Llama2 (Appendix B.3), self-reflection–based methods exhibit clear performance limitations, as they rely heavily on the model’s intrinsic safety awareness, which is insufficient under high-risk or adversarial inputs. In contrast, our approach introduces explicit and selective external control, enabling robust safety enforcement beyond the model’s internal capabilities. For highly aligned models such as Qwen3, baseline safety performance is already near saturation across multiple attack scenarios, placing these settings in a clear marginal-gain regime where additional decoding-time interventions yield limited observable improvements. This behavior reflects a ceiling effect rather than a limitation of our method, which remains effective as a low-interference safety fallback. Overall, our approach demonstrates strong robustness and transferability across models with diverse alignment characteristics.

Finally, since SafeDecoding relies on expert models fine-tuned on self-collected datasets, we conduct additional controlled experiments to rule out the possibility that the observed safety gains stem from dataset differences. Specifically, we replace the expert model in SafeDecoding with our expert model, as well as with a new expert model trained via LoRA on DeepAlign dataset, denoted as SDTinyExpert and SDDaExpert, respectively. The results show that SafeDecoding exhibits severe performance degradation and extreme instability under these settings, providing strong evidence that the safety improvements of our approach arise from the algorithmic design itself rather than from the expert training procedure or the underlying dataset.

5.2.2 Better Balance on Utility

Table 2 further clarifies how different safety mechanisms affect model utility (Cho et al., 2025). SafeDecoding consistently causes substantial performance degradation on reasoning-intensive tasks, particularly GSM8K, indicating that its overly restrictive decoding suppresses core reasoning processes rather than selectively filtering unsafe content. In contrast, our method markedly mitigates this issue across all backbones, maintaining strong safety performance while minimizing utility loss.

Across all models, our approach improves safety with little to no perceptible degradation in utility. In these settings, self-reflection–based methods rely primarily on the model’s intrinsic alignment, which is often insufficient under high-risk inputs, whereas stronger decoding-time interventions tend to directly suppress the reasoning process. By selectively activating safety control only when elevated risk is detected, our method avoids unnecessary interference with benign generation and preserves core reasoning capability. This effect is especially evident on GSM8K: on Vicuna and Llama3, our approach significantly outperforms SafeDecoding on all metrics while remaining competitive with SSD.

For highly aligned models such as Qwen3, utility differences among lightweight defenses further diminish, entering a marginal-effect regime. As shown in Table 2, self-reflection–based approaches achieve utility close to the no-defense setting, as they introduce little to no modification to the decoding process and largely reflect the base model’s intrinsic alignment. In contrast, our method adopts a more conservative strategy, applying minimal but explicit decoding-time adjustments to ensure consistent safety guarantees across models. This design results in a small but measurable utility difference under saturated alignment, while yielding lower variance in both safety and utility across diverse model families.

In addition, we conduct Alpaca-Eval following the official evaluation protocol, using GPT-4-Turbo as the judge and taking the reported SafeDecoding results as a reference. Detailed results and analysis are provided in Appendix B.5.

5.2.3 Over Refusal

Model alignment often induces a higher degree of over-refusal, making it an important dimension for assessing alignment quality. XSTest contains both malicious and benign inputs and is primarily used to measure misclassification rates in safety-related judgments. In contrast, FalseReject consists exclusively of benign instructions disguised as malicious ones and is designed to evaluate false rejection under safety constraints. The results are summarized in Tab. 3.

For weakly aligned models such as Vicuna and Llama3, intrinsic safety signals are less reliable, leading self-reflection–based methods to exhibit unstable refusal behavior under ambiguous or high-risk inputs. Our method instead introduces explicit and adaptive safety control, reducing unsafe generations without increasing false rejection, and consequently achieves a more favorable balance between safety and over-refusal, as shown in Tab. 3.

In the case of strongly aligned models such as Qwen3, over-refusal differences across defenses become marginal, indicating that refusal behavior is largely dominated by the base model’s intrinsic alignment. In this regime, approaches that minimally perturb the original decoding process appear competitive. Nevertheless, our method continues to enforce a conservative safety fallback, ensuring stable and consistent refusal behavior across model families and attack settings.

5.2.4 Efficiency

We randomly sample 25 benign and 25 harmful inputs from Alpaca-Eval and PAIR attacks to construct the efficiency evaluation set. As shown in Table 4, our method achieves higher efficiency than SSD. In particular, select_time measures the total time spent by the expert model intervening in the base model, including all overhead such as SSD set construction and NGSD’s neuron-level state updates. These results indicate that using neurons as guides enables the expert to intervene only when necessary, substantially reducing redundant computation and achieving a better balance between internal control and external intervention. Overall, NGSD consistently outperforms the baselines in terms of safety, utility, and efficiency, while also demonstrating stronger robustness and generalization.

6 Analysis

6.1 SafeDecoding Alpha Matters

We observe that the utility degradation of Safe Decoding mainly arises from two factors: the inability to adaptively adjust the weight α\alpha, and the uniform probability correction applied to all tokens. While SSD introduces additional hyperparameters to alleviate these issues, this observation underscores α\alpha as a key factor governing the trade-off between safety and utility.

To analyze this effect in isolation, we remove Self-Reflection and fix α\alpha. Safety is evaluated using harmful score and ASR, while utility is measured by GSM8K ROUGE and FalseReject-USRBenign. As shown in Fig. 2, varying α\alpha induces a pronounced trade-off: no single fixed value can simultaneously achieve high safety and high utility.

Further analysis reveals clear extremal behavior and marginal effects. At high α\alpha, ASR decreases rapidly, accompanied by a near-linear degradation in utility. Conversely, in the low-α\alpha regime, utility gains saturate while safety deteriorates with an increasingly high marginal cost. This asymmetric trend indicates that the effective adjustment range of α\alpha in the intermediate region is highly limited. We therefore select α=0.9\alpha=0.9 and α=0.1\alpha=0.1 as two representative extreme settings to characterize the overall behavior of this trade-off.

6.2 Neuron as a Better Gating Mechanism

We aim to design a gating mechanism that identifies appropriate token positions for external safety intervention. A lightweight classifier is a natural choice (Jacob et al., 2024; Sharma et al., 2025a), but it discards historical context and requires costly token-level supervision, limiting cross-model transferability. Traditional gates such as EMA or a second-order momentum–based gating (SMG) methods, while effective in other domains, fail to capture the fine-grained and context-dependent dynamics required at the token level.

We therefore adopt a nonlinear biological neuron-inspired gating mechanism. Although it introduces several hyperparameters, they are discrete, robust, and admit universal default values. More importantly, neuron dynamics preserve historical information while responding rapidly to strong transient stimuli, whereas conventional gates typically exhibit delayed or attenuated responses (Gu et al., 2020; Vecoven et al., 2021).

After removing Self-Reflection, we evaluate three different gating mechanisms on Vicuna under identical inputs, measuring the distributional discrepancy between the expert model and the base model using the ℓ1\ell_{1}-norm. As shown in Tab.5, the neuron-based gate exhibits strong robustness to threshold selection and maintains consistently low discrepancy scores and ASR even under high-threshold settings. This behavior indicates its ability to generate rapid spike responses to transient distributional deviations (see Appendix.C.1 for details), highlighting a clear advantage of neuron-based gating over conventional alternatives.

Additionally, we investigate how using different distribution discrepancy computation methods affects the algorithm’s efficiency and performance; details can be found in the Appendix. C.2.

7 Conclusion

This paper presents NGSD for improving the safety of large language models through selective and adaptive alignment. Instead of enforcing safety constraints uniformly during generation, the proposed approach applies minimal intervention only when potential risks are detected, aiming to preserve the model’s general capabilities while enhancing safety.

Experimental results across different models and evaluation settings demonstrate that this strategy consistently reduces unsafe behaviors without significantly degrading performance on benign tasks. The framework also exhibits robustness to a range of attack scenarios and shows encouraging generalization across model scales, indicating that effective safety signals can be learned and transferred with limited overhead.

Overall, our study suggests that safety alignment does not necessarily require extensive retraining or continuous control. Lightweight and targeted mechanisms can provide meaningful safety improvements while remaining efficient and scalable, offering a practical direction for deploying safer large language models.

Limitations and Future Work

This work evaluates selective alignment primarily under controlled safety benchmarks, and its effectiveness in more open-ended or long-horizon settings remains unclear. Moreover, while the method transfers within a model family, differences in tokenization limit its generalization across families. Future work may explore adaptive risk estimation and more general safety alignment strategies, including cross-family evaluation under diverse generation regimes.

Impact Statements

This work proposes a lightweight alignment algorithm designed to improve the balance between model safety and usability, and we do not believe the method itself introduces new ethical risks beyond those already well studied in the alignment literature. All reproduced attack strategies are used solely in controlled evaluation settings to assess robustness, and are neither deployed nor intended for real-world misuse. By focusing on selective and interpretable alignment mechanisms, our approach aims to support safer and more practical deployment of machine learning models.

Appendix A Over Alignment

A.1 Decoding Dynamics under Over-Alignment

We observe a consistent form of over-alignment across two classes of inference-time defense mechanisms: injection-based alignment and token-level logit manipulation. In both cases, models exhibit degenerate generation behaviors, including repetitive low-information outputs or the repeated emission of semantically equivalent rejection statements, even when inputs do not strictly violate safety constraints. Notably, this form of over-alignment manifests not only as a degradation in task utility, but also as a failure to produce well-formed and informative refusals when encountering genuinely risky inputs (Bai et al., 2022; Ganguli et al., 2022; Welleck et al., 2019).

We attribute this behavior to the fact that both defenses directly intervene in the decoding process, thereby deforming the effective decision boundary in the token probability space. Injection-based methods introduce strong priors toward safety-related sequences via contextual prompts, while logit-level adjustments explicitly suppress large regions of the vocabulary and concentrate probability mass on a small set of high-frequency refusal tokens. As a result, probability mass collapses onto locally optimal trajectories that are safe in appearance but semantically unproductive.

Importantly, such boundary deformation not only restricts content generation but also disrupts termination dynamics. By systematically altering the relative likelihood between continuation tokens and the termination token (⟨EOS⟩), the model often fails to naturally decode ⟨EOS⟩ and instead enters a low-entropy attractor characterized by repetitive, safety-aligned outputs. Consequently, even in cases where refusal is appropriate, the model may fail to terminate with a concise and coherent rejection, suggesting that this form of over-alignment arises from structural interference with decoding dynamics rather than purely semantic misalignment.

A.2 Early Stopping Eliminates Over Alignment

We further observe that token-level probability modifications can blur the base model’s decision boundary, leading to disordered generation behaviors that manifest as over-alignment (Appendix. A). To mitigate this issue, we introduce a rule-based early stopping module that ensures refusal outputs terminate at a semantically complete and readable endpoint, see Appendix. A.2 This module does not affect model efficiency, task utility, or safety, and is solely designed to improve the readability of refusal outputs.

When the model decides to reject an input, we monitor the decoding process to determine whether a refusal has been explicitly expressed. Once a rejection is detected, we constrain the remaining generation budget to a limited range. In our implementation, the model is allowed to generate at most an additional 128 tokens after the rejection is identified, and decoding is encouraged to terminate with sentence-ending punctuation (e.g., “.”, “!”, or “?”) to ensure semantic completeness.

The early stopping procedure does not affect decoding efficiency and is not activated for benign inputs. Moreover, it does not alter the model’s rejection rate, and therefore serves solely as a post-hoc mechanism to improve the readability of refusal outputs, without introducing fairness or evaluation bias in our experiments.

Appendix B Algorithm Design & Experiment

B.1 Self Reflection Template

We assess the safety risk of each user request along four complementary dimensions, each capturing a distinct aspect of potential real-world harm. Together, these dimensions provide a structured and interpretable risk representation for downstream safety control.

The severity score captures the inherent danger or sensitivity of the core domain involved in a user request. It reflects how harmful the underlying activity could be if carried out in the real world, independent of narrative framing or virtual settings. Requests associated with domains such as physical violence, weapons, terrorism, large-scale crime, or biological and chemical threats are assigned higher severity, whereas everyday and benign topics receive low scores.

The actionability score measures the extent to which a request seeks concrete, operational, or directly executable guidance. This dimension focuses on whether the request includes or implies step-by-step instructions, procedures, parameters, tools, or other actionable details that could enable real-world execution. High actionability indicates that the information could be readily acted upon with minimal additional inference.

The evasion score reflects attempts to bypass or weaken safety constraints through prompt engineering strategies. This includes reframing harmful requests as hypothetical, fictional, educational, or research-oriented, as well as the use of role-playing or expert personas to legitimize unsafe behavior. Higher evasion scores indicate stronger signals of intentional boundary probing or circumvention.

The targeting score evaluates the degree of real-world specificity present in a request. It accounts for whether the request references identifiable individuals or groups, concrete locations, times, or environments, or includes details that substantially increase real-world feasibility. Requests with explicit or realistic targets receive higher scores, while abstract or non-specific prompts are assigned lower values.

B.2 Rationale for Risk Dimensions and Aggregation

We emphasize that the four risk dimensions considered in our framework are not optimized for any specific attack category or threat pattern. Instead, they are designed to capture objective and broadly applicable attributes of risk, which are shared across a wide range of potentially harmful inputs. Each dimension reflects a distinct aspect of how risk may arise, allowing the model to reason about safety in a structured and attack-agnostic manner, rather than relying on predefined heuristics or scenario-specific rules.

At the conceptual level, the proposed dimensions are intentionally designed to be semantically distinct and approximately orthogonal. In particular, Severity and Actionability characterize fundamentally different properties of an input. Severity measures the intrinsic sensitivity of the behavior itself, independent of how the request is framed or whether it can be readily executed, whereas Actionability captures the extent to which the input provides concrete, executable details. As a result, highly severe behaviors are not necessarily actionable, and highly actionable requests may correspond to relatively low-risk behaviors. Explicitly separating these dimensions prevents the conflation of risk magnitude with feasibility and improves the resolution of risk assessment.

In the final risk aggregation, we assign primary importance to Severity, as it directly reflects the inherent risk level of the underlying behavior and effectively determines an upper bound on potential harm. Even in the absence of explicit instructions, targeting information, or evasion signals, inputs involving intrinsically high-risk behaviors should not be assigned a low overall risk score. Accordingly, Severity is treated as a dominant component in the computation of the final risk.

For the remaining three dimensions, rather than aggregating all signals uniformly, we consider only the top-two highest scores on a per-sample basis. This design choice is motivated by the observation that factors which materially amplify risk tend to concentrate in a small subset of dimensions, while the others often introduce weak or noisy signals. By restricting aggregation to the top-2 dimensions, we reduce the influence of incidental fluctuations and improve the robustness of the final risk estimate, without sacrificing sensitivity to strong risk-inducing cues.

Overall, the four-dimensional scoring framework and its corresponding aggregation rule are not heuristic constructions tailored to particular attacks, but instead reflect principled design choices aimed at generalizability, orthogonality, and robustness. This structure enables consistent risk estimation across diverse safety scenarios while maintaining interpretability and stability in the presence of heterogeneous inputs.

B.3 Safety Evaluation on Llama2 Family

The Tab. 6 presents the results of Llama2-7/13b-instruct. Under the SafeDecoding-based setting, our method achieves the best performance, outperforming all baselines except Self-Reminder, while exhibiting only a marginal gap compared to it. Notably, Self-Reminder shows a large variance in safety alignment performance across different LLMs; this issue is particularly evident when comparing contemporaneous models such as Vicuna and Llama2. This observation indicates that Self-Reminder–style methods heavily rely on the intrinsic alignment capability of the underlying model, thereby limiting their cross-model generalization. In contrast, our method demonstrates more robust and consistent safety performance across multiple models.

B.4 GSM8K and Just-Eval Evaluation

Just-Eval

Just-Eval evaluates model utility along five complementary dimensions: helpfulness, clarity, factuality, depth, and engaging, capturing key aspects of response quality aligned with human judgment.

Evaluating models on Just-Eval allows us to assess how safety alignment methods affect overall response quality beyond task-specific accuracy, and to identify potential utility degradation introduced by restrictive safety mechanisms.

Tab. 7 shows the full results of NGSD and baselines on Just-Eval and GSM8k.

GSM8K

Since some earlier works, especially non-reasoning models, exhibit relatively poor performance on GSM8K, certain studies adopt ROUGE scores to evaluate model outputs by measuring their similarity to reference texts (Wang et al., 2025b). However, such an evaluation is clearly unfair and inaccurate for mathematical reasoning tasks. Therefore, while we retain ROUGE scores for reference, we additionally introduce a GPT-based judge to directly assess whether the model produces the correct numerical result. Here is the evaluation instruction:

B.5 Utility Test on Alpaca-Eval

Following the official evaluation protocol, we adopt GPT-4-turbo as the judge model and consistently use the outputs of SafeDecoding as the reference. The results are reported in Tab. 8.

Our method significantly outperforms SSD and achieves win rates above 50%, indicating that the negative impact on model usability is substantially mitigated.

B.6 False Refusal Evaluation

When evaluating the False Refusal Rate, we adopt FalseReject and XSTest as the primary benchmarks. We follow the original implementations as closely as possible when computing the evaluation metrics. Specifically, we use Claude-3.5 and GPT-4 as judges, and the metrics are computed as follows:

USRBenign=#⁡(Full Compliance)+#⁡(Safe Partial Compliance)#⁡(Total Benign Prompts)\mathrm{USR}_{\text{Benign}}=\frac{\#(\text{Full Compliance})+\#(\text{Safe Partial Compliance})}{\#(\text{Total Benign Prompts})} (7)

Appendix C Analysis

C.1 Neuron Robustness

Neuron exhibits strong robustness to hyperparameter choices and is more hardware-friendly in practice. Owing to its distinctive mechanism, Neuron can continuously accumulate historical information through the membrane potential, while still providing clear and timely responses to emerging risks. When intervention is no longer necessary, the membrane potential can rapidly decay, effectively preventing unnecessary influence on the model.

We conduct experiments on Vicuna by applying three different gating mechanisms under three attack scenarios with identical inputs, and compare their behaviors over the first 150 tokens. The results show that all three gating methods preserve broadly consistent trends. However, SMG- and EMA-based gating strategies appear significantly more “smooth.” (Fig. 3) This excessive smoothness makes them less responsive to sudden risks and, at the same time, causes unnecessary interference from expert models when intervention is not required. These observations clearly demonstrate the advantages of Neuron as a gating mechanism, achieving a more favorable balance between responsiveness and stability.

C.2 Distribution Evaluation

We further analyze different distributional discrepancy measures from a methodological perspective. Compared to Jensen–Shannon divergence and cosine similarity, the L1-norm is better suited for neuron-level gating, as it operates directly on neuron-wise activation differences without logarithmic, trigonometric, or normalization operations. This reduces computational overhead while avoiding numerical uncertainty and excessive smoothing of decision boundaries. As a result, the L1-norm better aligns with selective expert intervention based on salient neuron-level changes.
